Oh please. This is not a concern. It basically pertains to adapting policies to the way people actually behave. For example, they found that sending a text message to lower-income students reminding them to do certain paperwork they need to do ended up increasing their college enrollment by 5.7 percentage points. As another example, they send outreach letters to farmers to remind them of a new loan program they may not have been aware of, which resulted in a 22% increase in farmers getting those loans.

Nobody at any point was forcing low-income students to enroll or forcing farmers to get those loans, nor was it coercing them to do so by making them miserable. It's applying well understood and scientifically rigorous insights about human behaviour into the real world to optimize policy outcomes. People aren't always rational actors, and even a simple rephrasing of instructions on a form or the repositioning of a checkbox can make statistically significant differences in aggregate.

Fault bad policies all you want, and I'll fault them right along with you, but applying what we know about human behaviour to implement policies is not a concern whatsoever. To the extent that there is any concern it is with specific bad policies themselves. Otherwise you might as well oppose making DMV forms easily accessible and easily readable in an online PDF because you oppose aspects of the DMV itself. Yeah the DMV sucks and could be improved, etc., etc., but if someone comes along and says "Let's make their forms accessible online, because many people would end up filling their forms on time if they could easily access them" is not being a totalitarian helicopter nanny just because the forms pertain to an aspect of government that sucks.
